q: Did the authors use an external test dataset?
hint: Look whether an independent dataset was used to test the model.

q: Did the authors report whether they used an existing model or developed their own?
hint: Look at the end of the introduction, aim is often stated there.

q: Did the authors report whether their code, model and data are open source, with a permanent link?
hint: Typically at the end of the paper, e.g. a 'Code availability' section.
Are computational resources (GPU, OS) and data openness described in sufficient detail?

q: Was transfer learning applied, and if so, accurately described?
hint: If TL was performed, is there a permanent link to the original and/or updated model?

q: Are all hyperparameters for model training specified to allow reproducibility?
hint: Check common ones: learning rate, train/val split ratio, early stop criterion.

q: Did the authors use performance metrics beyond the most obvious ones?
hint: Accuracy and AUC alone do not allow a full appreciation of model performance.

q: Did the authors go beyond performance to assess explainability / interpretability / transparency (XAI)?
hint: Might be in methods or discussion. Relieves the rat race on model performance alone.

q: Did the authors report on missing data and how it was handled?
hint: Missing data should be transparently described in methods to avoid bias during training.

q: Did the authors report their rationale for using AI?
hint: Not every method calls for brute AI force. Were the authors mindful about their use of AI?

q: In case of classification, did the authors report on class imbalance?
hint: Class imbalance might drive model bias. A 99:1 dataset is 99% accurate by always predicting the majority class.

q: Is it immediately clear from the title that this paper involves AI?
hint: For later systematic reviews and immediate transparency on the use of AI.

q: Was the specific type of AI elaborated on?
hint: E.g. unsupervised / supervised / reinforcement, which type of machine learning method.
